record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses an emergent-misalignment fine-tuning scenario to evaluate its own mitigation method. Its reported outcomes are ethical-alignment scores on benign questions, not the refusal, harmful-compliance, token-position, or parameter-localization measures named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for its emergent-misalignment mitigation framework and related alignment-method comparisons. These are related to the claim's subject but do not test any listed version's specified behavior or measure. Background results cited from other studies are not recorded. Code-hacking task accuracy is a capability measure, not a safety-behavior measure.
record.test_reason: The paper evaluates its own emergent-misalignment mitigation method (self-assessment plus DPO) on Qwen3-4b during code-hacking fine-tuning. Its only outcome is an LLM-judged ethical alignment score on 24 benign questions. It reports no harmful-request compliance or refusal rate, no per-token KL, no prefill or decoding attack, no parameter localization, and no depth-of-alignment training. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that EA maintains high alignment scores in the code-hacking emergent-misalignment scenario without a significant capability tax. They note it is limited in detecting latent sleeper agents before activation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates a self-assessment plus DPO alignment framework in an emergent-misalignment scenario; it does not apply the original harmful fine-tuning/refusal, per-token KL, or compliant-prefill methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports minimal divergence when changing among four self-assessment prompts. It also reports different outcomes for sleeper behavior before versus after activation.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 5 runs on Qwen3-4b after the code-hacking emergent-misalignment scenario, Emergent Alignment scored PFAS 91±0.7. No alignment scored 85±2.1, and the other methods scored 86–90.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent-misalignment mitigation methods differ in LLM-judged ethical alignment on benign questions after code-hacking fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors say hybrid SFT+DPO training showed no alignment-score reduction versus SFT only (figure only). They also report recovery to alignment from every misalignment checkpoint.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-assessment DPO during fine-tuning preserves or restores judged ethical alignment in the code-hacking scenario.

fits_no_version.finding: Divergence across the four self-assessment prompts was minimal; the authors call the prompt's effect negligible.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The choice of high-level ethical self-assessment prompt has little effect on judged alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: The method did not detect the sleeper agent before activation, but did align it after activation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-assessment alignment responds to active but not latent backdoor behaviour.

record.code_released: If the paper is accepted, code will be made available under an open source licence.
record.problems: The alignment outcome is assessed by Qwen3-30b-a30b rather than human raters; the authors note that it can score some responses as mildly misaligned despite no apparent human-standard misalignment. The key figures are supplied only as figures in this text, without numerical values. The reported sleeper-agent results are limited to the stated test scenario.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4's code-hacking evaluation accuracy was left out because it measures task capability rather than safety or ethical behavior. Cited results from other papers were not extracted as this study's results.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance are not measured.
The paper does fine-tune on code hacking, but it reports no harmful-request compliance and no pre- versus post-fine-tuning safety comparison.
Per-token KL by response position is not measured.
Prefill, suffix and decoding attacks are not tested.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks is tested.
The causes of shallowness are not examined.
No training that spreads safety past the first tokens is tested.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.05946) only in passing, as background. Two internal inconsistencies stand out. First, the text says four 'other' prompts were tested, yet only four prompts are listed in total. Second, the authors say the judge scores 85–90 even for non-misaligned responses, which makes the 85 no-alignment baseline in Table 1 hard to read as erosion. The evaluation questions are benign, and the measure is ethical alignment rather than harmful-request compliance. Figure values are not given numerically.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-request compliance or refusal rate is measured; the paper does not test a few-to-hundreds harmful examples as the safety intervention.
No ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning dataset is tested for its effect on harmful-request compliance.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.
No compliant-opening prefill, suffix attack, or decoding change is tested for harmful-request compliance.
No test localizes safety behavior to weights, parameters, or ranks.
The study does not test why safety behavior would be shallow or whether data or training objectives produce shallowness.
The study does not train or evaluate safety behavior spread beyond the first tokens, or test whether such deepening holds up.
